To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
ParA exists as a monomer-dimer in equilibrium that is shifted by ATP toward a dimer that binds DNA.

the ParA protein exists as a monomer-dimer in an ATP-dependent equilibrium, that the more active form of ParA in the DNase I protection assay is the dimer, that the effects of ParA and ATP concentration on DNA binding can be explained as a direct result of the oligomerization equilibrium, and that ATP is not absolutely required for DNA binding, but rather stimulates the equilibrium in the direction of the more active form.
ParA exists as a monomer-dimer complex that can bind to the par promoter, that ATP stimulates ParA binding to the par promoter and that ATP hydrolysis may be required for dissociation.

the mechanism of ParA DNA binding, and we have shown that ATP is not required, but does enhance, DNA binding activity.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ParA protein binds DNA in an ATP-stimulated, but ATP-independent manner.

ParA is an ATP-dependent DNA binding protein, that the ATP binding and hydrolysis are not required for DNA-binding, but rather the ATP-dependent oligomerization of ParA is the primary determinant of its DNA binding activity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ParA is an ATP-dependent DNA-binding protein, that the ATPase activity is required for DNA binding, and that ParA exists as a dimer in solution.
ParA is a DNA binding protein that exists in a dynamic equilibrium between monomeric and dimeric forms.
ATP is not required for ParA DNA binding but is required for ParA oligomerization.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ATP-dependent ParA protein is a dimer that binds to the par promoter.
the ATPase domain of the ParA protein is important for the DNA-binding activity of the full-length protein.
ParA is an ATPase that binds to DNA in a site specific manner and that ATP is required for ParA to form dimers.
